subject: desertOasisDiorama
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: desert oasis with palms, tents and camels.
Style: low-poly whimsical mix.
reasoning:
I'm planning a desert oasis diorama with palms, tents, and camels in a whimsical low-poly style, keeping the module robust and moderately long since I can't test the SDK directly. Since camels are creatures, I'll build them skeleton-first with proper joints, while treating props like tents and palms as simpler static objects.

I'm sketching the layout: a base disc roughly 2.4m wide with camels around 0.4m tall, using a root joint at the origin that everything else parents to, plus a helper function for placing parts. For the terrain I'm planning a faceted sand-colored cylinder base with layered dune shaping and height-based coloring.

Next I'm adding an oasis pond at the center with a teal ripple-textured disc, surrounded by rocks and a flattened grassy ring, and three palm trees around it with tapered trunks and arching fronds built from extrusions or bent sweeps to keep the geometry simple but stylized.

I'm working through the geometry so the width stays perpendicular to the flow direction, giving a flat feathery blade shape viewed from the side or above, while the card's face orientation along flow determines whether it reads as edge-on or broad-faced depending on viewpoint.

I'll go with lean 70 and bend 50 so each frond reads as a thin curved profile, with fronds radiating at different azimuths so some are always seen face-on from any viewpoint. I'm setting up a per-frond flow function tied to frame index, sizing the cards around 0.34 by 0.5 with a frond texture drawn as a green rib-and-leaflet SVG gradient rather than relying on tinting.

For solidity I'll add a crown boss sphere and small orange sphere clusters for dates, skipping extra extruded rachis geometry to keep things simple. The trunk itself will be a sweep along a catmull curve with a tapered radius, painted with brown ring stripes along the y-axis for bark texture, and I'll keep these props jointless since sway isn't needed here. Now I'm moving on to designing the tents, starting with a Bedouin-style striped pavilion for the first one.

For tent A I'm using a radially-segmented cone with angular stripe paint computed via atan2 around a center point, a cylindrical wall base, a conical striped roof with flaps, a dark arched doorway decal facing front, a pole with an extruded pennant flag on top, and guy ropes running to pegs on the ground. Tent B will instead be a wider ridge-style tent built by extruding a gable/triangle profile to form an A-frame shape.

I'm also planning an awning in front of tent B using a tilted box part, choosing terracotta/cream stripes for tent A and teal/cream with gold trim for tent B, and now moving on to designing camels — a reusable `camel` function building jointed standing camels (maybe an adult and a smaller baby one) with unique joint names parented to the root.

Since joints stay unscaled and only meshes carry scale, I realize I need to compute camel geometry in local coordinates using a transform helper that applies yaw rotation, scale, and translation to each point, keeping orientation-dependent parts minimal by relying mostly on points-based shapes like spheres and capsules for the body, hump, and eyes.

Now I'm working out the actual local coordinate values for the camel: scaling the diorama to roughly 1:4 of real camel proportions so the hump stands about 0.5m tall, with the body built as a sweep along a spine chain from hips to chest, and making sure the lowest points of the feet sit exactly at the ground plane y=0.

Still defining the chain structure...

Settling on 'hipLCalf' for naming, then sketching the body as a swept spine chain with tapering radii from rump to chest, plus a transform helper applying scale, yaw, and translation to each point.

Now I'm sketching the neck as a camel-like S-curve of points rising from chest to head, chained as neck1, neck2, etc., parented off the last spine joint.

For the head, I'm placing a head joint oriented forward-and-down toward a target point, with a separate jaw joint for the lower jaw, plus skull sphere, muzzle box, ear spheres, eyes, nostrils, and lip details layered on top.

Adding muzzle and jaw capsule geometry...

I'm giving it a single dromedary-style hump, and thinking about adding a draped saddle blanket over the torso using a loop sweep around a spine joint, though I'm wary of it accidentally intersecting the legs.

Maybe add tassels and a striped blanket cap just for the main camel, with the calf getting a simpler bow instead. For the legs, I'm thinking through IK chains with shoulder joints and foot targets, using three-segment limbs with specific lengths so the knees bend naturally rather than staying perfectly straight.

Working through leg bend directions...

For front legs, elbow bends back while the knee bends forward since the carpal faces forward, so I'll flip the hint directions relative to the hind legs. I need to make sure these hint vectors get rotated by the same yaw transform applied to the root and target positions in model space.

For the limb chain, I'm setting up four points giving three spans plus a tip joint, naming them hip, knee, ankle, and foot so the bone chain assembles correctly. I'm sweeping each chain with a tapering radius array and adding a flattened sphere as a foot pad at the tip joint, colored dark tan, with the foot's target height set low to keep it planted near the ground.

Now I need to decide the parenting: the hind legs attach to the hip joint on the spine, and the front legs attach to a further spine joint, while the neck comes off the end of the spine and the tail branches off a different root joint. I want to confirm the spine's joint count matches the catmull-rom spans so these parent references line up correctly, and I need to make sure the camel's feet rest on a flat part of the base without dunes interfering.

I'm defining a dedicated hips joint positioned at the rear of the spine for leg attachment, then building the body as a sweep along the spine chain with a radius function scaled by the overall size factor, rounding the caps at each end. The neck gets its own sweep tapering from a wider base to a narrower tip, positioned so its base tucks inside the body for a seamless joint, and now I'm settling on a sandy tan fur coloring approach for the camel.

Now I'm working out the facial features: small dark spheres for eyes with highlight dots, tiny cone ears tilted outward, dark nostril spheres at the muzzle tip, and simple capsule shapes for eyebrow ridges, deciding to keep things simple rather than adding decals or lash geometry. I'm also planning small tufts of hair on the head and chin, a tail with a tuft at the end, a tuft on the hump, and dark knee pad spheres, before moving to build the calf using the same approach.

Thinking through the baby camel proportions, I decide against overcomplicating with a separate head-scale system and instead settle on just scaling the whole body down with a smaller size constant, accepting that it's close enough to look cute without needing a fully separate head-anchor-relative scaling function.

For the overall scene, I'm planning two camels total (one standing near the tents, one calf near the pond) at roughly 45 parts each, plus supporting props: sand dunes, flattened rock shapes, a couple small cacti, palm trees and a bush, water jars and crates near the tent, and a campfire made of a stone ring, glowing flame cones, and logs using the glow kit.

I'm also considering a hanging lantern with a glowing window, and a patterned magic carpet rug laid flat on the sand near the tent as a whimsical textured detail, possibly with tassels. For a finishing touch, I might add a crescent moon finial on a pole atop the tent instead of a full sun backdrop.

For the pond, I'm picturing lily pads with a lotus flower, surrounding reeds and grass tufts as card elements, and maybe a trail of camel footprint decals leading from the edge of the diorama to the water for extra charm.

I'm also thinking about the base: layered strata colored by height with a sandy top band, plus a small "OASIS" name plaque sitting on the front rim as a decorative box with a textured face.

Checking the edge math, the curve at that radius comes out to about 1.377, close enough to 1.4 for the plaque to sit flush with a slight protrusion of 0.02 and thickness 0.05.

Scaling the base to a 2.8m diameter, I'm comparing proportions: palms at 1.1m, the camel around 0.66m, tent at 0.55m, making sure the palms remain the tallest element as intended. Now I'm working out the lathe profile for the base shape, defining the bevel points to get a flat top with a slight curved edge.

For texturing, I'm painting strata by vertex height, assigning darker brown near the bottom and alternating sandy band colors going up, with the top surface getting a mottled sand look based on normal direction. Then I'm adding dunes using scaled hemisphere geometries placed around the ground, positioning one toward the back-left and planning more to fill out the terrain within the base radius.

Checking the dune placements, I realize some extend beyond the base circle's radius when accounting for their scale and position, so I'm recalculating centers and scales to keep every dune's extremities within the 1.4 unit boundary.

I want a shared sand paint function that blends two sand tones using noise and adds ripple lines across both the top surface and dunes for a cohesive textured look.

For the pond, I'm placing a thin cylinder as the water surface slightly above ground level, with a separate textured circle on top to render ripple detail.

Now I'm planning the overall scene layout from a front-facing camera view: oasis pond left-center, palms around it, tents back-right, camels front-right, with +X mapped to screen-right. I'm placing the pond at an offset position with an elliptical shape and surrounding grass ring, then starting to position the palm trees around it.

I'm positioning three palm trees at varying heights and lean angles around the pond, plus a small sapling near the water's edge. Then I'm placing two tents (a round striped one and a gable-style one) on the right side, with camels and a calf positioned in front of them.

Now I'm working out tent door orientations facing toward the pond, plus a campfire location between the tents and water, while rechecking the pond's ellipse dimensions since the ring radius is making it too large for the grass island base.

I'm reworking the tent placements, putting the striped tent at (0.65,-0.55) and a smaller gable tent at (1.0,0.1) facing away, plus a campfire near (0.55,0.25). Now I'm figuring out camel positions near the pond and computing the yaw angle so the first camel faces toward the water.

I'm adjusting positions to avoid overlaps—shifting the rug near the camels, repositioning the campfire relative to the pond ring, and placing jars, crates, cacti, and rocks around the tents. Now I'm working out the back dune's placement and scale so it extends properly in the z-direction without colliding with other elements.

For a whimsical touch, I'm considering adding a crescent moon and a string of small triangular bunting flags sagging between tent A's pole and palm P2's trunk, built with a catmull sweep and tiny flag extrusions along the curve.

I'll pass explicit bone references through the along-path calls to keep flag placement consistent. For Tent A, I'm planning the geometry as separate pieces: an 8-sided cylinder for the walls and a cone for the roof, sized relative to the tent's radius and wall height.

For the striped paint pattern, I'm computing each point's angle around the tent's center using atan2 on world coordinates, then bucketing into 8 segments to alternate colors — this keeps the stripes continuous across rotated parts since it's based on world position rather than local geometry. I'm checking that the cone's radial facets align with these same 8 angular divisions so the roof stripes match up with the wall stripes below.

Now I'm working on a scalloped valance around the roof's edge, planning to place a ring of small cone or wedge shapes pointing outward/downward around the roof perimeter using a radial frame function to position each piece.

I'm also sketching the finial (pole, gold ball, pennant flag, crescent) and figuring out how to place the door as a flat arched plane on the correct wall facet, computing its position and facing direction based on the facet's yaw angle and the wall radius.

For the door's orientation, I need to pick an angle that aligns with one of the octagonal facet centers (22.5° plus multiples of 45°), then choose the facet that roughly faces toward the pond—calculating the direction vector from the tent to the pond gives roughly -55.6°, so I'm rounding to the nearest valid facet angle of -67.5°.

Actually for better front visibility I'll simplify to -22.5° so the tent faces mostly forward. I'm sizing the door panel to fit comfortably within the facet width, positioning it at the correct wall height, and now need to make sure the cone roof's base radius extends beyond the wall for proper overhang.

Working through the yaw rotation math for tent B's gable extrusion, computing the rotated x-axis direction and cross product to get the correct thickness direction for the extrude call.

I'm deciding faces get solid cream paint while the slanted roof gets stripes based on position along the forward axis, and adding a door texture on the front wall. I'm also planning a second tent variant with ridge pole ends topped by golden balls and a tilted awning plane supported by poles near the entrance.

Working out the awning's extrusion geometry...

For the campfire I'm planning a ring of stone dodecahedra, crossed log cylinders, and glowing cone flames, plus a tripod kettle setup for extra story detail. I'll also add a lantern on a pole near the tent door with a lathe-built body and a soft glow.

Nearby I'm placing jars with painted stripe patterns, crates, and a sack on the right side of tent A. For the rug, I'm building a flat plane with an SVG pattern -- bordered rectangle, diamond medallion, and fringe lines -- working out the correct orientation so the pattern faces up and reads correctly from the front.

I'm adding a small cushion pair on the rug, skipping footprints, and setting up the pond with lily pads, a lotus flower, and surrounding rim stones using low-detail dodecahedron geometry scaled flat for a natural rock look.

Now I'm placing reeds and grass tufts around the pond rim using SVG-textured billboard cards, and defining a palm tree function that builds a curved leaning trunk from a series of swept points.

I'm adding bark rings, a flared base cone, and a crown with clustered date/coconut spheres plus nine frond cards arranged radially around the trunk's top point, each angled outward and slightly drooping to read as palm fronds.

Now I'm splitting the fronds into an upper set of five with a shallower lean and curl versus a lower drooping set of six with steeper lean and bend, giving the crown a layered look. For the frond texture, I'm drawing an SVG with a central rib and rows of tapered leaflet blades along both sides, shading root-to-tip from dark to light green.

Writing SVG leaflet polygons...

With sizing settled at 2px/unit for a 256-tall texture, I'm planning the texture set: frond, grass tuft, reed, two door variants, rug, water ripples, sign plaque, giving roughly nine textures total, which fits the 5-12 target. I'll skip a separate camel eye SVG and just use spheres instead, then move to importing the glow helper from the kit for the next step.

For glow I'll use it on flame, lantern glass, and embers, but need to watch that painted materials can't glow so those need flat colours instead. Materials are shared per colour string, and since flat colours count toward a 64 limit while paints don't, I'll lean heavily on paints — sand, base, grass, palm trunk, tent stripes, camel coat, water, rocks, wood grain, cloth — and reserve flat colours for things like gold, ink, white, flame hues, and lotus accents, keeping the total well under the cap at around 30.

I'm also thinking through paint atlas resolution: total painted area is roughly 12 square meters, so I want higher texel density and will bump paintSize to 2048 so the atlas stays crisp without exceeding the 4096 ceiling.

Now I'm starting the actual build script, setting up imports from the builder library and its glow kit.

Writing import list and type declarations...

Adding a helper function to simplify part placement, working through the typing for optional parameters so TypeScript accepts the spread cleanly.

Pragmatic typing is fine since `any` is allowed here. I'm sketching helper functions for rotation vectors, a vector type alias, geometry shape helpers like spheres and rocks, then defining color palette constants for sand tones...

Writing sand paint shader...

Still writing color logic...

Now I'm defining the paint textures for grass, wood, and rock surfaces, using mottled and grain patterns with distinct color pairs for poles versus planks, and layering a lighter countershade on rock tops.

Then I'm designing stripe-based paints for cloth and tree trunks—a radial stripe helper for tents, and a nested trunk paint combining wood-tone stripes with a darker countershade overlay. For the camel coat I'm combining a mottled tan base with a soft countershade to give it warm highlighting.

Now I'm defining the camel-building function, setting up a transform helper that rotates body points by the given yaw angle and translates them to the camel's position and scale, plus a direction-vector helper that applies the same rotation. I'm double-checking the rotation math so that the local forward and right-hand axes map correctly onto world space for whatever yaw the camel faces.

Next I'm building the skeleton: a hips joint tagged with a "spine" role, followed by a spine chain built from a Catmull-Rom curve through several points along the camel's back, split into three segments. Then I'm starting the body sweep that profiles the torso's width and height along the spine using a sine-based taper, applying the coat color to the surface.

Adding the hump sphere attached to the spine joint, sized and positioned to sit toward the back, considering whether a smaller second hump makes sense or if a single dromedary-style hump with a tuft is more fitting.

Now I'm layering darker hair spikes on top of the hump and shaping a partial-sphere blanket cap over the body, positioning and scaling it to cover the upper region while leaving the underside open, then thinking through adding stripe patterns to the blanket.

I'm defining horizontal stripe bands by y-axis for the blanket coloring, then setting up a girth loop around the body's spine to sweep a drape band around the midsection.

So rx should align with body-length width and ry with surface thickness, meaning binormal maps to body axis and normal maps to surface normal. For the joint loop, I'm checking that the plane through the joint's point works for finding the surface loop around the body mesh, though I need to watch for cases where the loop might be missing and throw an error.

To guard against that, wrapping the risky loop calls in try/catch seems like a safe approach, accepting that some features might silently skip if something fails. For the camel's extra details, I'm deciding to skip the saddle bag and pack but add a blanket cap, girth, and tassel cones at the hump base. For the tail, I'm sketching a catmull chain of points running from the rump down toward the ground to define its curve.

Now I'm building the tail chain with a tapering sweep radius and a small spike or sphere tip at the end. Then I'm setting up the neck as its own catmull chain attached to the spine, giving it an S-curve shape that rises and bends forward before sweeping it with a tapering radius too.

Adjusting the neck endpoint higher for better camel proportions, then defining the head joint at the top of the neck with its own origin and direction, plus a local coordinate function for scaling head features. Writing skull sphere code...

Still placing facial features...

Adding a lower lip sphere at the muzzle tip, a forehead tuft spike pair, and checking that the muzzle and skull spheres overlap smoothly in radius. Now I'm defining the leg builder function, setting root and foot positions scaled by side and front/back offsets.

For the foot, I'm aligning the pad sphere so its bottom sits flush with the ground target, adjusting the pad scale and offset so there's no gap or overlap. Then I'm working out the limb segment lengths needed to span from the root joint down to the foot, checking the thigh, shin, and lower segment lengths sum enough to allow a natural bend with the last segment roughly vertical below the knee.

Now I'm setting up the bend direction hints for the leg solver and writing the chain call with joint names for hip or shoulder, knee, hock or ankle, and foot, distinguishing front versus hind limb naming conventions.

Defining sweep radii...

Adding a small chest fur spike cluster, then adjusting calf proportions and coat lightness. I'm sketching out the palm tree generator function that builds a curved trunk from points leaning toward an azimuth, ready to add the crown next.

Writing trunk sweep code...

I'll taper the ring radius from wide to narrow using lerp, scaling the torus geometry to about 10 rings total. Then I'll add a dark brown crown boss sphere at the top, five hanging date spheres arranged in a circle with orange and brown coloring, and start building the frond geometry arrays.

Writing frond card logic...

Good, so several fronds stay visible from any camera angle. Now I'm working out the tent geometry — building cylindrical walls with painted radial stripes, aligning facet boundaries so each 45° segment gets its own color band.

Adding roof cone and valance scallops...

Still shaping the flag swallowtail polygon, then positioning the door plane on its angled facet with correct orientation and dimensions.

I'm adding guy ropes and pegs radiating from the eave outward to the ground at several angles, skipping those near the door, plus considering a small emblem for the tent.

Now moving to a trim ring at the wall base for added detail, then starting tentB's design with teal and cream stripe paint logic based on face orientation, and adding gold trim rods along the front triangle edges for visual accent.

I'm defining a coordinate helper to map local (u,v,w) offsets to model-space points using the right and forward vectors derived from yaw, then outlining the tent's cross-section shape and extruding it to form the body. I'm placing the door texture on the front face and starting to position trim rods along the front edges.

Now I'm adding more rods for the ridge pole and apex, with gold end caps, then setting up an awning plane attached above the door that slopes outward and down from the front face using a blended forward/up direction vector.

I'm checking that the awning's attach height and slope keep its lip above the door opening, since too low a position would block the door — settling on attaching around the gable's upper region and sizing the drop so the lip clears the door top, then computing support pole positions from the lip corners down to the ground.

Now I'm defining the awning's painted surface and its geometry: setting up a sloped outline so the stripe pattern follows the fabric, verifying the slope direction is orthogonal to the width direction, and adding a row of small downward-pointing cones along the lip edge as a decorative valance.

I'm also sketching out lathe profiles for the jars, plotting radius-height coordinate pairs that bulge outward then narrow to form a closed revolved shape back to the axis.

For paint, I'll apply banded stripe patterns varying by height for terracotta and blue-glazed jars, giving each a distinct colored finish. For the crates, I'm using simple box geometry with a wood-paint texture and dark bands, stacking two together and adding a small squashed-sphere sack with a tied spike on top for variety.

Skipping the barrel to keep things simple. For the campfire, I'm placing three leaning log rods radiating toward a center point, surrounding them with a ring of eight small rock-colored dodecahedra stones, and adding glowing layered flame cones in orange, yellow, and pale gold.

A tripod of three thin poles leans inward to meet above the fire, holding a chain that suspends an iron cauldron lathed from a rounded profile, positioned just high enough to clear the flames.

I'm also planning a lantern on a curved hook-pole near tent A's door, built from a hexagonal glass prism with warm glow, gold cap, and base disk, plus a small rug near tent B's entrance and a wooden sign plaque on the front of the base.

For the plaque, I'm figuring out placement on the lathe-generated circular base, adding a textured plane facing outward with "OASIS" text and a palm icon, plus some simple palm glyphs as a backup in case the font rendering doesn't come through clearly. Now I'm thinking about adding a lotus inside the pond.

I'm working out the lily pads as small flat green cylinders, then figuring out a water ripple texture drawn on a scaled plane with pale arcs and sparkle highlights so it reads as shimmering water, and sizing the elliptical water surface itself.

Still shaping the grass island...

I'm layering the water surface above the sand with rocks edging the pond rim, and planning palm tree positions scattered around the island with one leaning toward center and a sapling nearby.

Checking each palm's distance against the grass ellipse boundaries confirms most sit comfortably within range, with P2 slightly outside but still plausible standing on sandy edge terrain.

Now I'm placing small grass disc patches at each palm base for ground detail, then working out tent B's position and orientation—setting its yaw angle and center point, then calculating the forward and back extent corners to make sure the footprint plus awning fits within the scene bounds.

I'm checking tent A's footprint and ropes stay within the overall radius limit, then measuring the distance between tent A and tent B centers to see whether their outer edges and awning extents overlap—comparing A's edge toward B's back corner against their combined radii.

Repositioning B to (1.0, 0.0) and A to (0.55, -0.68) to fix that near-overlap, I verify A's reach plus rope allowance stays under the limit and that B's back corner clears A. Then I'm placing the campfire around (0.42, 0.2) and checking its distance from B's awning lip to make sure it doesn't collide with the tent structure.

Now I'm working on the rug placement, trying to fit it between the campfire and camel 1 without overlap, and testing camel 1's position and facing angle to keep its extended body and width clear of the fire — nudging it to around (0.45, 0.88) with a steeper yaw to resolve the edge collision.

I'm also positioning the calf relative to its mother, considering a few facing directions so it looks natural turned toward the viewer, and checking its distance and body length against nearby elements.

Then I'm placing cacti at distances that keep them spaced out properly, and building each one with capsule-shaped trunk and arm segments with curved sweeps for a more organic look, including some mottled green coloring and flower details.

Next I'm positioning the dune hemispheres with scaled and rotated placements, checking their distances from the palms so nothing overlaps.

I'm setting up the hemisphere geometry with scale and rotation parameters, favoring flat shading for a low-poly facet look on the dunes. Now I'm placing rocks near the pond and working out bunting connections between tree P2's trunk and tent A's pole, estimating their heights for the attachment points.

Computing the sagging bunting rope as a quadratic bezier curve between trunk and tent pole points, then sweeping a thin rope geometry along it and generating triangular flags along the path...

Still writing flags...

Checking the overall proportions — path length, flag spacing, and direction alignment all seem reasonable. I'll skip extra embellishments like a crescent finial, footprints, or birds to keep the scene from getting too cluttered.

Now I'm tallying up the total part count: palms, camels, tents, fire, pond, and misc details add up to roughly 400 pieces, well under the 1000 limit, so I'm fine there. I'm also listing out the texture names I'll need — FROND, TUFT, REED, DOOR_A, DOOR_B, RUG, RIPPLE, SIGN — plus a plaque texture, which covers everything.

Writing frond SVG code...

Shading leaflets with a gradient from dark base to lighter tip, then starting a separate tuft of grass shape.

Designing six curved blades of grass using quadratic bezier paths, each with a slightly different tip position and color...

Now I'm sketching the reed element with three tapered stalks plus a brown cattail capsule, followed by an arched doorway with a dark interior.

Now designing a second door variant with a pointed arch, teal curtains, and a gold crescent moon emblem, then moving to the rug design with a red base, cream and navy border bands, a central gold-teal diamond medallion, corner triangles, and fringe details at both ends sized to match the overall scale.

For the ripple effect I'm adding stroked white ellipses and small sparkle stars with varying opacity, keeping most elements fairly visible above .7 opacity, then starting a transparent-background sign element.

Writing OASIS text with bold serif styling, decorative palms, a dark outline stroke, and a wood-plank backdrop beneath it, with camels left as plain untextured spheres. I'm planning to build the base first since every part already has color assigned, so I can skip worrying about color fallback logic.

I'm setting up the lathe profile for the base shape, checking that the x-coordinates never go negative and that the outline loop closes properly along the axis, then applying sand coloring continuously across the rim and top with a slightly darker "ink" edge for the rounded rim detail.

Now I'm checking relative scale -- comparing camel height against the tent and palm sizes to make sure the diorama proportions feel realistic, since real camels are roughly two-thirds the height of a typical tent, and I want the models to reflect that ratio rather than making the camel too large.

I'm settling on a camel scale factor of 0.9 and tent height of about 0.5, with tent entrances proportionally smaller than the camel so it still reads as a toy-like scene, and the palm fronds topping out around 1.3-1.45 units overall so the subject area reads as the tallest, most prominent part of the composition. I'm also double-checking joint and chain naming conventions across the camel's skeleton -- spine, neck, hips, shoulders -- to make sure each generated joint name stays unique even when calf/variant tags are appended.

Now I'm writing the sweep functions for the spine and neck, using radius functions that taper along the length, plus helper functions for building body parts (spikes, spheres for the tail tuft, lashes) with consistent bone attachments and coloring.

Still writing camel details...

Adding a cheek strap and a bell on a neck collar, positioning the torus using the chain point's axis and bone data.

I'm considering whether the door needs its own glow geometry versus relying on a plane with a bright color texture for that lit-up effect.

For orientation, I'm reasoning through which "up" vector to use for vertical planes like the rug versus walls, making sure the texture faces the right way relative to the viewer and the tent's yaw rotation.

Good, right-side orientation checks out, not mirrored. I verify the door plane orientation the same way, confirming the viewer's right matches the computed local X axis. With orientation math settled, I'm ready to write out all the code, including a helper for lathed parts.

Setting up imports from the builder library and the glow kit, defining basic constants and a seeded random function for things like rock sizing...

Now I'm laying out the flat colour palette for the scene — gold, ink, cream, red, teal, rope, pad, hair, dark eye, white, pink, and flame tones.

Rounding out the palette with more flame, amber, date, leaf, and navy/blue shades for about 25 paint colors total, then setting up a radial stripe helper that paints angular bands around a center point based on atan2 angle calculations.

For the two tents, I'm picking contrasting color schemes: tent A with red/cream radial stripes on the roof paired with blue/cream stripes on the walls, keeping it playful but balanced.

Setting up the build function now, defining helper closures for placing parts and rods with consistent bone attachment and radius-then-color ordering...

Writing the lathe-based base shape, then layering flattened hemisphere dunes positioned flush with the base's top surface so they blend in without z-fighting.

For the pond and grass patch, I'm stacking two scaled cylinders—a wider grass disc and a smaller water disc nested on top, offset slightly in height so the water appears recessed just above the grass surface.

Now I'm adding a rim of small jittered rocks circling the pond's ellipse, and planning reed clusters positioned along the back-left arc of the pond using angle ranges to keep them clustered naturally.

I'm also scattering grass tufts around the island and placing lily pads at slightly offset positions near the pond center for a natural clustered look.

Now I'm designing a lotus flower on one pad, arranging six outward-tilted cone petals in a ring around a yellow spherical core, then starting to write the palm tree generator function that builds trunk points from position, height, angle, and lean parameters.

For placing fronds along the trunk, I'm deciding to safely sample points and tangents directly from the path curve at fixed intervals rather than relying on a possibly unavailable `t` property in the sweep callback.

Still writing frond generation code...

I need to fix the TypeScript typing on the flow callback so it infers correctly, and make sure frame() returns a proper point/direction pair. Then I'll move on to defining a tent structure function taking center coordinates as its next piece.

Writing tent geometry code...

Placing small decorative cones along each octagon facet...

Positioning the door at an angle offset from center, then placing the pole with a gold ball ornament at the apex and a small flag extending outward to suggest wind direction.

For the guy-ropes, I'm placing eight of them around the tent at the cone vertex angles, running from the eave down to pegs on the sand, keeping all of them even near the door since they frame it without blocking entry. Now I'm moving on to writing the code for Tent B following this same plan.
